chapter_theme: The friend shows the waiting wife the rainy season he promised to return by, reading cloud, lightning, thunder and the flowers of the mullai woodland as proof that he will come (1-18); then the man, his king's work done, turns home (19-20).

1.reading: The friend says that the man who promised 'we will come' when the rainbow lay across the sky like the garland on the chest of Mal, the god coloured like the warring sea, and sweet rain hung low, can hardly fail to come now that the sky, its clouds massed, roars and pours.
1.nuance: The question வாரார்கொல் ('will he not come?') is reassurance put as a doubt, and the promise is quoted in his own word, வருதும். The mullai god Mal lends the rainbow his garland, so the season he swore by arrives with a sacred sign.

thinai_evidence.note: the rainbow and the massed, roaring rain clouds fix the rainy season he named

comparisons.tenor: the rainbow lying across the sky, like the garland on Mal's adorned chest

2.reading: As the fierce sun grows poor and the rain grows rich, and the long forest puts out shoots on every branch, the friend tells the heroine of the curved earrings that the lovely sky flashes its lightning, carrying his message: 'our man will come at once.'
2.nuance: Sun and rain are cast as a poor man and a rich one, the very terms of the journey he made for wealth. The lightning is made his envoy (தூது), so the absent man's word reaches her through the sky.

thinai_evidence.note: the rain's season and the long forest

comparisons.tenor: the waning sun and the growing rain, as a man grown poor and a man grown rich
the lightning, which speaks as the absent man's envoy

3.reading: Showing her own distress, the friend says that the striped paathiri is withering, the wind cuts through, hail rolls over the fine sand of the cool woodland and the thundering sky pours down and rises again, as if all of it, since yesterday, were aimed at one lone woman.
3.nuance: ஒருத்தி, 'one woman', is the heroine seen from outside: the storm that should promise his return is felt as an assault on her alone. The colophon says the friend shows her own inability to bear it so that the heroine will bear hers; the comfort is left unspoken.

colophon.thurai: பருவங் கண்டழிந்த தலைமகள் ஆற்றல்வேண்டித் தோழி தனது ஆற்றாமை தோன்ற வுரைத்தது

thinai_evidence.note: the cool woodland and the thunder of the rains

4.reading: The friend tells the heroine of bamboo-smooth shoulders that the peacocks put on their finery like dancing women, the konrai has bloomed and made the forest lovely, and this season, when singing bees hum, is the medicine for her wasting pallor.
4.nuance: The friend does not say he has come; she says the season is the cure, because the season was his promise. The sign is made to stand in for the man.

thinai_evidence.note: the konrai and the season of bees, the rains he promised

comparisons.tenor: the peacocks spreading their plumes
the season, as the cure for her pallor

5.reading: The friend tells the heroine whose eyes are like arrows that the return of the man who left fearing the words of those who scorn is no lie: here the woodland is such that red velvet-mites crawl over it like scattered coral.
5.nuance: He went because of others' contempt, the contempt shown to the poor; the friend answers that talk with a proof that does not talk, the season's red insects on the ground.

thinai_evidence.note: the velvet-mite of the first rains on the mullai woodland

comparisons.tenor: the heroine's kohl-lined eyes, long and piercing as arrows
the red velvet-mites scattered over the woodland

6.reading: Seeing her shoulders so wasted they cannot hold bangles, the friend tells the heroine, whose wide eyes are like a split tender mango, not to grieve: the sky thunders fiercely along the long road, telling those who went, 'do not delay.'
6.nuance: The thunder speaks to the absent man, not to her: the friend makes the season his summons, so the comfort is that he too is being told. The variant நெறியிடை for நெடுவிடை does not change the sense.

thinai_evidence.note: the thunder of the rains

comparisons.tenor: her wide eyes, like a tender mango split down the middle
the thunder, as a voice that orders the absent man not to delay

7.reading: The friend tells the drooping heroine that the rain, flashing on every side like the fire of a famous sacrifice kept without lapse, will bring back the man who went to make himself able to give to those who seek him and to crush those who oppose him.
7.nuance: His purpose is given as the two duties of a puram hero, giving and punishing (ஈதல், தெறுதல்). The sacrificial fire tended without lapse lends the rain the same steadiness: the season keeps its rite as he will keep his word.

thinai_evidence.note: the lightning and rain of the season

comparisons.tenor: the lightning flashing on every side

8.reading: The friend tells the heroine, good in all a woman's ways, that the woodland, where the kaayaa has opened its fine buds, blue as if dipped in the collyrium of an eye, announces the return of him who parted seeking fame that lasts in this world made of earth.
8.nuance: மண் இயல் ஞாலத்து மன்னும் புகழ், lasting fame in a world made of earth, sets the permanent against the perishable. Here the friend makes his reason honour, not wealth, and lets the season answer it.

thinai_evidence.note: the blue kaayaa of the mullai woodland in the rains

comparisons.tenor: the dark blue kaayaa blossoms

9.reading: Flowers have bloomed like eyes, the glory lilies on their rain-fed stems have taken on their finest beauty, and, speaking many sweet words, they announce the return of the man who left her so that the striped bangles slip from her forearm.
9.nuance: The flowers are given the friend's own task, sweet words of reassurance (இன்சொல்). Which flower line 1 names (உருவினை) is not clear.

thinai_evidence.note: the glory lily that blooms in the rains

comparisons.tenor: the season's flowers, opening like eyes
the flowers, as speakers of the friend's sweet words of comfort

10.reading: While the thunder roars in the sky and the strong, quarrelsome bull of the herd bellows back at it in anger, the swift-horsed chariot comes with the sound of a forest river, so that my friend's body will freshen like a new leaf.
10.nuance: வானேறு and ஆனேறு pair the thunder, the sky's bull, with the bull of the herd, which challenges it. The chariot is heard before it is seen.

thinai_evidence.note: rain-season thunder answered by the herd's bull

comparisons.tenor: the sound of the approaching chariot
the thunder, as the sky's bull, which the herd's bull takes for a rival
her body freshening like a tender shoot

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the verse names the heroine in the third person (என்தோழி), so it may be spoken in her hearing to others

11.reading: The friend tells the heroine of the curled, five-plaited hair that the woodland, where the kodal has put out clusters like the raised heads of snakes, announces the swift return of the man who went to bring the wealth that makes their union possible.
11.nuance: புணர்தரு செல்வம், 'wealth that brings union', is the friend's gloss on why he left: the wealth was for their life together, not against it.

thinai_evidence.note: the kodal opening in the rain-fed woodland

comparisons.tenor: the kodal flower-clusters raised on their stems

12.reading: The friend tells the heroine of kohl-dark lovely eyes and peacock-like grace that his coming, shown by a sign beyond doubt, is certain: every day the dark clouds, like elephants anointed with oil, rise on the right.
12.nuance: ஐயந்தீர் காட்சி: the friend offers an omen as proof. Clouds rising on the right (வலம்) are a good sign, and they rise every day, so the sign is renewed daily.

thinai_evidence.note: the dark rain-clouds rising daily

comparisons.tenor: the heroine's grace
the dark, glistening, massive rain-clouds

13.reading: The friend tells the heroine of the lovely raised waist that the rain hangs down as lovely as her hair, which her lover delights in, and the clouds flash lightning that dazzles the eye like the clashing swords of kings cutting down elephants.
13.nuance: A battlefield is lent to the sky, kings' swords flashing among elephants, so the war that keeps the hero away is seen again in the weather that should bring him home. Whose hair line 2 means, and whether காதலர் goes with it, is not clear.

thinai_evidence.note: the lightning and hanging rain of the season

comparisons.tenor: the rain hanging down in dark strands
the lightning flashing in the clouds

14.reading: The friend tells the heroine of shining jewels that they are sure their lover, who went to bring wealth, will come quickly: the fragrant cool rain-cloud laughs softly and sweetly as the mullai puts out its bright teeth.
14.nuance: The mullai buds are teeth and the cloud laughs with them: the season smiles, and the friend reads the smile as the answer to her doubt. தெளிந்தாம், 'we are certain', is the friend's word.

thinai_evidence.note: the mullai buds of the rains

comparisons.tenor: the mullai buds, as bright teeth
the rain-cloud, as one who laughs

15.reading: The friend tells the heroine of well-made jewels that her lover is not one to abandon her: it is the season when, lodged within the clustered kurunthu blossoms, the bee sings in the ili mode and the large bee plays its sweet flute.
15.nuance: உள்ளுறையாக here means 'lodging within' (the bee inside the flowers); it is the word the grammar uses for the hidden comparison, but nothing in this verse is hidden. The insects' lute-note and flute make the woodland a concert for the season of return.

thinai_evidence.note: the kurunthu, a mullai tree, in flower

comparisons.tenor: the bee's hum, as a song in the ili mode
the large bee's drone, as flute playing

16.reading: As the black koel falls helpless, the great peacock dances and the loud sky thunders, the friend tells the heroine of broad shoulders that the pallor on her body, tender as young asoka shoots, will grow stale and pass.
16.nuance: The koel, a bird of the spring, loses heart when the rains come while the peacock dances: one season's voice gives way to another's, as the pallor of waiting should give way to his return.

thinai_evidence.note: the thunder of the rains

comparisons.tenor: the heroine's body

17.reading: On the high hill of rock ledges the thunder crushes the snakes; with thunder voiced like a drum the sky has drunk the sea and, pouring, has thickened the dark; and the simple girl's brow has taken on the beauty of the crescent moon.
17.nuance: The last line turns from storm to face: the brow that pallor dimmed has its crescent shape and light again, because the rain promises him, so the friend reads the cure on the heroine rather than in the sky.

thinai_evidence.note: the cloud that drank the sea pours and darkens the sky

comparisons.tenor: her brow, regaining the crescent's shape and glow
the thunder, voiced like a drum
the cloud, as a drinker of the sea

18.reading: The friend says that, to announce the return of those who crossed the stony forest, the thunder of good sound stands there in mid-sky, and the forest, which was as dull as a poor man's body, has put forth beauty like a rich man's mind.
18.nuance: The forest has made the journey the man is making, from poverty to wealth. The two similes set the poor man's body against the rich man's mind: wealth shows inwardly as gladness, poverty outwardly as drabness.

thinai_evidence.note: rain-season thunder over the woodland

comparisons.tenor: the forest putting forth its beauty in the rains
the forest, drab before the rains

19.reading: The man, his work done, tells his charioteer that the red-stemmed maraa has blossomed on its flowered branches, white like the plough-bearing god, and his heart has already gone the long way ahead, wanting as its companion the woman whose forearm shines with green bangles.
19.nuance: The heart sent ahead of the chariot is the returning hero's figure; தோடுணையா வேண்டி, 'wanting her as companion', makes the heart a traveller of its own on the road the chariot has yet to cover.

thinai_evidence.note: a man returning from his work to a waiting wife, the mullai situation

comparisons.tenor: the white blossom of the maraa

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the addressee is the charioteer (பாகன்); the colophon names the speaker தலைமகள், but the verse is the returning man's (see source_issues)

20.reading: The returning man says the glorious king's work is finished and the roads have turned pleasant to travel, while the rain-cloud moves on with its thunder like the army of warring kings, so that the gem-bearing serpents wilt.
20.nuance: The army he has left is seen again in the sky: the cloud marches home like the troops of kings, as he does. The serpent that shrinks at thunder is the thunder's mark, not a sign of its own.

thinai_evidence.note: the roads made pleasant by the rains

comparisons.tenor: the rain-cloud moving on with its thunder

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the addressee is the charioteer (பாகன்); the colophon names the speaker தலைமகள், but the verse is the returning man's (see source_issues)

links.note: Mullaippattu 1-6 likens the rain-cloud rising from the sea to Mal, who grew to measure the world; Kar Narpathu 1 likens the rainbow to the garland on the chest of Mal, coloured like the warring sea.
links.teaches: Both mullai poems open their rains with Mal, the god of the mullai land, so the land's god is the first image of its season; the later venba moves him from the rising cloud to the rainbow, making the sky his adorned chest rather than his growing body.

links.note: Akananuru 85: the friend tells the heroine not to weep, since the rain now spreading is the season he named when he assured them 'வருதும் யாம்'. Kar Narpathu 1 quotes the same promise, வருதும், and asks 'will he not come?'
links.teaches: The promise is the same word in both, which shows the friend's argument as a fixed form, quote his 'we shall come' and point to the rain, with the older poem supplying the peacock calling its mate as the proof the four-line verse leaves out.

links.note: In Mullaippattu the old women seeking an omen hear a herd girl tell the calves 'இன்னே வருகுவர் தாயர்' and take it as a sign; in Kar Narpathu 2 the lightning speaks his message, 'இன்னே வருவர் நமர்'.
links.teaches: The same formula of reassurance, 'they will come at once', is an overheard chance word in the idyll's omen rite and the sky's own message in the venba, so the later poem turns the ritual of listening for a sign into the season speaking for the absent man.

links.note: Both carry the same thurai, the friend showing the season to reassure the heroine, with the konrai in bloom; Akananuru 4 ends with his chariot in sight, Kar Narpathu 4 with the season as medicine for her pallor.
links.teaches: Set together they give two endings to one speech: the long poem can produce the man himself on the horizon, while the four-line venba has to stop at the season and so makes the season itself the cure.

links.note: Kar Narpathu 4: the season is the medicine for her pallor. Kural 1265: the pallor of her soft shoulders will leave only after she has seen her husband with full eyes; on a plain reading the two disagree about what cures pasalai.
links.teaches: The friend claims the sign of his return heals the pallor and the Kural's woman holds that only the sight of him will, so the couplet reads as the heroine's answer to the whole method of the Kar Narpathu's friend.

links.note: Kar Narpathu 5: he left fearing the words of those who scorn. Akananuru 111: the friend says he will come back, ashamed of the mocking words of hostile men (ஏஎச்சொல் நாணி).
links.teaches: Taken together, other men's contempt both sends the hero away for wealth and, in the friend's argument, drives him home again, so shame works on him at both ends of the journey.

links.note: Kural 1263: she lives on, longing for the return of the man who went desiring victory with his resolve as his only companion. Kar Narpathu 7: the friend says he went to give to seekers and crush foes, and the rain will bring him back.
links.teaches: The couplet's woman treats his heroic aim as the rival that left her behind, while the friend names the same aim, giving and conquest, as a reason to trust he will return in the rains: one motive is a grievance in the Kural and a guarantee in the venba.

links.note: Verse 7 gives the purpose of his journey as giving to seekers and destroying foes; verse 8 gives it as lasting fame in this earthly world.
links.teaches: Read in sequence, the friend's account of his motive moves from duties toward others to fame for himself while her proof stays the same rain-season sign, so the series varies the cause of absence and holds the cure fixed.

links.note: Kar Narpathu 9: the flowers speak many sweet words announcing his return. Akananuru 74: the heroine tells the friend she could hold firm on her many sweet words of reassurance (வன்புறை இன்சொல் நன்பல) were it not for the herders' flute at evening.
links.teaches: Akananuru 74 gives the heroine's answer that the Kar Narpathu never records: sweet words of comfort hold her only until the evening flute, so the reassurance the venbas repeat is shown elsewhere to fail at its own hour.

links.note: Akananuru 134: the returning hero tells the charioteer that if she hears the sound of the swift-horsed chariot (கடுமான் தேர்ஒலி) there may be union at midnight. Kar Narpathu 10: the friend hears the swift-horsed chariot coming like a forest stream and says the heroine will bloom.
links.teaches: The chariot's sound is the hinge of the reunion from both sides: the hero hopes she will hear it and the friend reports that it is heard and what it does to the heroine's body, in the same phrase கடுமான் தேர்.

links.note: Both liken the opening kodal cluster to a snake's raised hood in the rain-fed woodland; in Akananuru 154 the returning man sees it from the chariot, in Kar Narpathu 11 the friend points to it as the sign of his quick return.
links.teaches: The same flower-image is seen by the man on the road home and offered by the friend at home as a promise, so the shared stock of mullai images lets the two halves of a separation read the same sign in the same season.

links.note: Kar Narpathu 12: dark clouds like oiled elephants rise on the right every day, a sight beyond doubt that he will come. Mullaippattu 4-5: the cloud drinks the cold sea and rises rightward (வலனேர்பு), just before the old women go out to seek an omen.
links.teaches: The idyll sets the rightward-rising cloud beside a separate omen rite, while the venba makes the cloud itself the omen 'beyond doubt', which shows the rising on the right read as a good sign for the absent man's return.

links.note: Akananuru 9 ends with the returning man asking whether his heart, which went ahead longing for her soft shoulders, has reached her; Kar Narpathu 19 has the man say his heart has gone the long road wanting her as companion.
links.teaches: Both returning heroes speak of a heart that outruns the chariot, so the figure belongs to the set speech of return; the long poem follows the heart into the house and to her touch, while the venba stops at its setting out.

links.note: Akananuru 44: the king has finished his work, the enemy has paid tribute, and the man bids the charioteer drive ahead to sleep on his wife's breast. Kar Narpathu 20: the glorious king's work is done, the roads are pleasant, and the rain moves like an army.
links.teaches: Both make the king's finished war the condition of the husband's return, and the pair shows the venba compressing the long poem's catalogue of kings and battles into one simile in which the rain-cloud marches like the armies he leaves.

links.note: Kural 1268: let the king fight and win; let us join the house and keep the evening feast. Kar Narpathu 20: the king's work is finished, so the roads home are sweet.
links.teaches: The couplet is the wish spoken while the war goes on and the venba is the same man once it is granted, so read together they give the before and after of one situation, the hero held by the king's war until it ends.

new_concepts.gloss: the season the absent man named for his return, which the friend points to as proof that he will come
new_concepts.label_source: the verse's word (Kar Narpathu 4, பருவம்) and the colophon's (பருவங்காட்டி)

source_issues: 19, 20: the colophon reads வினைமுற்றிய தலைமகள் பாகற்குச் சொல்லியது, but both verses are the returning man's speech to his charioteer (19: his heart goes to the woman with bangles; 20: the king's work is done); தலைமகன் is meant.
1 line 2: தீம்பொழல் is not a known word; தீம்பெயல், sweet rain, fits the sense (the variant gives வீழ for தாழ).
8 line 2: வால்கூறும் reads as a misprint for வரல்கூறும் (compare 9 line 3 and 11 line 2); line 4 நுண்ணுரும் பூழ்த்த is probably நுண்ணரும்பு ஊழ்த்த, fine buds opened.
9 line 1: உருவினை names no clear flower; the flower likened to eyes may be கருவிளை; the verse is marked uncertain.
13 line 2: கூந்தல வனப்பின் is hard to construe with காதலர் in line 1 (whose hair is meant is unclear); the variant ஏமாந்த for ஏமார்ந்த changes the lover's epithet.
15 line 3: திருந்தின் repeats line 1's திருந்தி and does not parse; the sense is taken from இளிவண்டு பாட.
16 line 4: பழங்கூண் is unclear (perhaps பழங்கண்); the sense that the pallor will fade is a guess, and the verse is marked uncertain.
